Immune-mediated retinopathy
in a patient with stiff-man syndrome
Abstract @ Background: Stiff-man
syndrome is a rare neurological dis-
order characterised by rigidity and
violent spasms of the body muscula-
ture. In the majority of patients,
presence of antibodies against glu-
tamic acid decarboxylase (GAD),
the enzyme synthesizing y-aminobu-
tyric acid (GABA), suggests an au-
toimmune attack against GABA-ergic
inhibitory neurons. We report a
32-year-old patient with stiff-man
syndrome and anti-GAD antibodies
who developed subacute progressive
loss of vision in the right eye, and in
the left eye 18 months thereafter.
@ Methods: Ophthalmological work-
up included electro-retinogram
(ERG), visual evoked potentials
(VEP) and fluorescein angiography.
Antiretinal antibodies were investi-
gated using an indirect immunofluo-
rescence technique on frozen sections
of macaque retina with patients se-
rum and FITC-conjugated goat anti-
human immunoglobulin. Staining
with monoclonal anti-GAD65 anti-
bodies and with serum from three
healthy normals served as controls.
@ Results: Visual acuity of both eyes
Introduction
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is a rare neurological disor-
der characterised by rigidity of axial and proximal limb
muscles superimposed by painful muscle spasms [15—
18, 21]. Despite significant functional disability, motor

Autoimmune pathogenesis of SMS is suggested by the
presence of auto-antibodies against glutamic acid decar-
boxylase (GAD), the y-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-syn-
thesising enzyme, in 60-80% of patients [25-27]. More-
over, high prevalence of at least one of a number of auto-

213
immune disorders (including insulin-dependent diabetes,
pernicious anaemia, vitiligo, Graves’ disease, Hashimo-
to’s thyroiditis, myasthenia gravis and autoimmune adre-
nal failure) has been demonstrated with SMS [12, 25, 26].
Oligoclonal bands are often found in the cerebrospinal
fluid (CSF) [26, 27]. Immune suppressive treatment and
plasmapheresis have shown some benefit [14, 22, 30].
We report a patient with longstanding stiff-man syn-
drome who developed severe bilateral visual deteriora-
tion. The data suggests that anti-GAD antibodies to
GABA-ergic retinal structures may be responsible for
the ophthalmic manifestations.
Case report
The patient’s symptoms began at the age of 14 years with progres-
sive stiffness and hyperlordosis of the lower spine. Vertigo, spells,
fever, nausea, vomiting and short periods of disorientation preceded
symptom onset by about 2 years. At the age of 19 years, jerky
spasms developed in the lumbar region. The spasms were extremely
painful, lasted 3-4 min and were generally characterised by opistho-
tonic posturing and severe diaphoresis. They usually occurred spon-
taneously in the morning, but were also provoked by cold, psycho-
logical stress or startling stimuli. Relief of spasms was achieved
with clonazepam. Despite cessation of medication, the patient re-
mained free of spasms over the following 3 years. Spasms and invol-
untary jerks reappeared at the age of 23, but could be controlled with
diazepam (5—10 mg per week). Gradual drug tolerance, however, ne-
cessitated increasingly higher dosages (80-100 mg/day).
At the age of 30 years, sensation of glare and visual loss to 0.16
in the right eye occurred over a period of 6 weeks. The patient was
initially diagnosed with optic neuritis and treated with intravenous
prednisolone (1 g/day) as recommended by the ONTT study group
[5]. Visual acuity, however, did not improve. Eighteen months later
the left eye was similarly affected.
Neurological examination
Examination revealed fixed kyphosis of the upper and hyperlordosis
of the lower spine; the paravertebral muscles were stiff and hyper-
trophic. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk in the lower extremities.
The remainder of the neurological examination was normal.
Imaging
Cranial computerized tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imag-
ing (MRI) of the cranium and spine, and thoracic myelography were
all normal. X-rays of the spine showed signs of scoliosis and decal-
cification of the lumbar vertebrae.
The patient died in 1997, about 12 h after a spasm-induced fall
involving head trauma. Autopsy was not performed.
Methods
Clinical and diagnostic work-up
In addition to a complete neurological examination including MRI,
ophthalmological examinations, electrophysiological tests as elec-
troretinography (ERG), pattern ERG, spinal tap, fluorescein angiog-
raphy, kinetic and static perimetry and laboratory evaluation (pres-
ence of anti-GAD antibodies in both serum and CSF, catecholamine
levels, standard serologic studies, glucose tolerance test) were per-
formed.
Visual evoked cortical potentials (VEP) were investigated with
standard diagnostic procedures using a television checkerboard pat-
tern (16x14 checks, check size 1°) presented to the subject with a
stimulus reversal frequency of 1.88/s. The border frequencies of
the amplifier were 0.5—250 Hz with an average number of 200. Elec-
trode placement was Oz (occipital central) versus Fz (frontal cen-

tral). Mean latency of the first prominent positive component was
101.03 ms+5.01 SD in a group of 47 normals.
ERG was recorded using ganzfeld flash stimulus in agreement
with the ISCEV standard, Arden gold-foil electrodes as well as stan-
dard amplification and signal filtering (bandpass 0.5—300 Hz, oscil-
latory potentials 70-300 Hz).
Assessment of antiretinal antibodies and immune histochemical
taining
Tissue preparation
Retinas were obtained from adult monkeys (Macaca fascicularis)
under deep sodium pentobarbital anaesthesia. After enucleation
and hemidissection of the globe, the retina was isolated in 0.01 M
phosphate buffer (PBS), fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 45 min
and processed for cryostat sectioning. Vertical retinal sections of
12 um and 14 um were taken from paracentral areas.
Immunohistochemistry
An indirect immunofluorescence technique was used according to
the following protocol: The vertical sections were rinsed in 0.1 M
PBS (pH 7.4) and preincubated for 1 h in a solution with 10% nor-
mal goat serum (NGS), 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA) and 0.5%
Triton X-100 in 0.01 M PBS (ph 7.4). The primary antibodies were
diluted in a solution containing 3% NGS, 1% BSA, 0.5% Triton X-
100, 0.5% sodium azide in 0.01 M PBS (pH 7.4) and the sections
were incubated for a period of 12 h. For double immunofluorescence
the sections were incubated in a mixture of two primary antibodies:
either patient serum (diluted 1:1000) and a monoclonal GAD65 an-
tibody (Boehringer Mannheim; 1:500) or serum of an unaffected
control patient (diluted up to 1:1000) and the monoclonal GAD65
antibody. After rinsing the sections several times in 0.1 M PBS
(pH 7.4), the sections were incubated in a mixture of two secondary
antibodies — a fluorescein-labeled goat anti-human immunoglobulin
(Dianova; 1:1000) and a CY3-labeled goat anti-mouse immunoglob-
ulin (Dianova; 1:500) — for a period of 4 h. The antibodies were di-
luted in 3% NGS, 1%BSA, 0.5% Triton X-100 in 0.01 M PBS. After
washing the vertical cryostat sections in 0.1 M PBS (pH 7.4), we
coverslipped them in Mowiol (Hoechst).
Fluorescence microscopy
Staining was visualised with a fluorescence microscope (Axiophot,
Zeiss) and photographed using different fluorescence filters (450-
490, FT 510 and LP 520 for fluorescein; BP 546, FT 580 and
LP 590 for CY3).

Results
Ophthalmological examination and follow-up
Upon admission in February 1996, visual acuity was 0.16
in the right eye and 0.6 in the left eye. Despite aggressive
immunosuppressive treatment with 1.v. steroids and meth-
otrexate, progression of visual loss in the left eye could
not be prevented. By May 1996 visual acuity of the left
eye had dropped to 0.3, and by August 1996 it was down
to 0.16. Visual acuity of both eyes then remained at 0.16.

Biomicroscopy and fluorescein angiography were nor-
mal on the initial evaluation and on follow-ups in May
and August 1996.
Static (Tiibingen Automatic Perimeter) and kinetic
(Goldmann) perimetry revealed a central scotoma of
about 10 deg in both eyes.
Colour discrimination, as examined by Ishihara’s col-
our plates, the Heidelberg anomaloscope and the Farns-
worth Panel D 15 test revealed a red-green deficit. Colour
discrimination was only moderately affected on the left
eye when the patient presented in February 1996 and pro-
gressively worsened.
ERG-recordings
The results of the ERG recordings are presented in
Figs. 14 and VEP recordings are summarized in Fig. 5.
Recordings of the right eye were abnormal at all times.
Recordings of the left eye showed gradual deterioration.
Abnormal electro-ocular responses were initially noted
on the pattern ERG (Fig. 1) and on photopic ERG
(Fig. 2), which revealed abnormal a- and b-waves in re-
sponse to photopic single red flash. Scotopic responses
(Fig. 3) became pathologic only later on. Increasingly ab-
normal flicker responses (Fig. 4) and the progressive im-
pairment of the photopic responses (Fig. 2) reflect the
progressive deterioration.
VEP recordings
On the first examination in October 1994, stimulation of
the left eye evoked a normal cortical potential, whereas
an attenuated VEP with normal latency was evoked from
the right. Repeated investigations revealed a mild but pro-
gressive slowing of the right eye VEP. VEPs for the left
eye remained normal until March 1996, when they first
desynchronised with a W shape. By the patient’s last visit
in August 1997, VEPs were about equally delayed and at-
tenuated on both sides. The progressive deterioration of
visual function is shown in Fig. 5.
Laboratory investigations
Standard serological studies, glucose tolerance tests and
repeat spinal taps yielded normal results except for one
oligoclonal band in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) on the
second tap in 1996. Norepinephrine, epinephrine and do-
pamine levels in the plasma and the CSF were within nor-
mal ranges. High levels of autoantibodies to both iso-
forms of GAD were present in patient’s serum
(167 432 U anti-GAD65 and 792 U anti-GAD67, RIA)
and to GAD65 in the CSF (2495 U, RIA).
Assessment of antiretinal antibodies

the macaque retinal inner plexiform layer and weaker

and displaced amacrine cells in the ganglion cell layer
were labeled. Testing was carried out five times (March,

GAD65 antibodies (Fig. 6C). Incubation with a control
serum of three unaffected patients did not result in any
staining (not shown).
Discussion
The typical clinical symptomatology and the presence
of anti-GAD antibodies in both serum and the CSF con-
firm the diagnosis of SMS. Two questions arise from
the signs of visual deterioration. First, what is the ae-
tiology of the visual loss, and second, is there any rela-
tionship to SMS? Despite the interval of 18 months, the
features of impairment indicate that both eyes were af-

fected by the same disease process. We focus on the
ERG recordings and the VEP of the left eye, enabling
us to closely monitor the disease progression. The first
electro-ocular responses to show marked abnormalities
were the pattern ERG and photopic single red flash re-
sponses [Fig. 1, Fig. 2 (top)]. At this time the VEP was
normal (Fig. 5). Colour discrimination was only moder-
ately affected. This pattern of impairment indicates the
retina as the primary site of the disease process and
rules out secondary retinal involvement due to an optic
nerve lesion. A primary optic nerve lesion, e.g. optic
neuritis, would have shown VEP abnormalities concur-
rent with symptom onset and more pronounced impair-
ment of colour discrimination. However, based on these
findings alone, it is difficult to specify which retinal
structures may have been afflicted initially.
The immunological findings suggest a disease starting
at the inner and outer reticular levels: the serum of our pa-
tient showed pronounced staining of the inner plexiform
layer with weaker staining of the outer plexiform layer.
Amacrine cells of the inner nuclear layer and displaced
amacrine cells of the ganglion cell layer were also la-
beled. Using the monoclonal anti-GAD65 antibody (in
place of the patient’s serum) resulted in a similar staining
pattern. However, while no difference was noted at the
level of the outer plexiform layer, the inner plexiform lay-
er showed slightly stronger reactivity with patient’s serum
than with the monoclonal anti-GAD65 antibody. This
could be due to the fact that the serum of our patient con-
tained both anti-GAD65 and, albeit to a lesser extent, an-
ti-GAD67 antibodies. The latter could be responsible for
the staining of (additional) retinal cells that express only
GAD67.
Due to the large amount of dendrites of amacrine cells,
the inner plexiform layer is strongly GABA-immunoreac-
tive (GABA-IR) [7, 20]. Approximately 40% of the ama-
crine cells in the human retina are known to be immuno-
reactive for the inhibitory transmitter GABA [7, 8, 20, 31,

218
32] and express the isoforms GAD65 and/or GAD67 [29].
These include the amacrine A17 cells, which form recip-
rocal synapses to rod bipolar cells, and starburst amacrine
cells, which synapse directly on ganglion cells [7, 23, 31,
32] and receive synaptic inputs from both the rod and
cone systems. A minority of amacrine cells express
GAD67 exclusively [29]. Some of these cells may have
contributed to the more intense staining pattern of the in-
ner plexiform layer seen with patient’s serum, which con-
tained both anti-GAD65 and anti-GAD67.
Horizontal cells, whose dendrites branch into the
outer plexiform layer, are also GABA-ergic [3, 4, 13].
In monkeys (and probably in humans as well) they ex-
press only GAD65 [28]. However, the concentrations
of GABA and GAD65 are much lower in horizontal
cells than in the amacrine cells [28, 29]. These findings
suggest that the antiretinal antibodies of our patient re-
cognize the same epitopes as monoclonal anti-GAD an-
tibodies. In other words, it is possible that the antiretinal
antibodies and the patient’s anti-GAD antibodies are
identical.
The clinical and electrophysiological findings of our
patient could easily be explained provided in vivo anti-
GAD antibodies bind to amacrine and horizontal cells
as well and inhibit GABA-ergic transmission by inhibit-
ing GABA synthesis. However, the possible role of the
anti-GAD antibodies in causing retinal disease and their
significance in SMS has yet to be elucidated [10]. How
can antiretinal antibodies reach their target when the
blood-retinal barrier is intact? It is possible that short-
term (e.g. transmitter-induced) disruptions of the blood-
retinal barrier may happen, as has recently been described
[6]. To date, there is no animal model that elucidates the
functional role of anti-GAD antibodies. However, an an-
imal model does exist for cancer-associated retinopathy
[2], which in terms of ERG findings and selective anti-
body binding to a specific target has some similarities
with the retinopathy of our patient. In that model, anti-re-
coverin antibodies were shown to pass through the intact
blood-retinal barrier, causing apoptosis of photoreceptors
[1, 2].
Finally, it is not known whether the large doses of
benzodiazepines taken by our patient may have contrib-
uted to the retinopathy. Benzodiazepines are strong
GABA-A receptor agonists [9, 23]. GABA-A receptors
are located on photoreceptor terminals, the dendritic
tips and axon terminals of bipolar cells, and on ama-
crine cells [11, 23, 31]. SMS patients are also treated
with baclofen, a GABA-B receptor agonist known to
enhance the light-induced acetylcholine release of ama-
crine cells in vitro [19, 24]. Nothing is known about the
long-term retinal effects of therapeutic levels of benzo-
diazepines or baclofen. One may speculate whether
these drugs contribute to, or prevent, impairment of ret-
inal function in SMS patients.
In summary, the data presented suggest that the reti-
nopathy in our patient may be due to anti-GAD antibodies
attacking the inner and outer plexiform layers.

segments.text:
Case report
The patient’s symptoms began at the age of 14 years with progres-
sive stiffness and hyperlordosis of the lower spine. Vertigo, spells,
fever, nausea, vomiting and short periods of disorientation preceded
symptom onset by about 2 years. At the age of 19 years, jerky
spasms developed in the lumbar region. The spasms were extremely
painful, lasted 3-4 min and were generally characterised by opistho-
tonic posturing and severe diaphoresis. They usually occurred spon-
taneously in the morning, but were also provoked by cold, psycho-
logical stress or startling stimuli. Relief of spasms was achieved
with clonazepam. Despite cessation of medication, the patient re-
mained free of spasms over the following 3 years. Spasms and invol-
untary jerks reappeared at the age of 23, but could be controlled with
diazepam (5—10 mg per week). Gradual drug tolerance, however, ne-
cessitated increasingly higher dosages (80-100 mg/day).
At the age of 30 years, sensation of glare and visual loss to 0.16
in the right eye occurred over a period of 6 weeks. The patient was
initially diagnosed with optic neuritis and treated with intravenous
prednisolone (1 g/day) as recommended by the ONTT study group
[5]. Visual acuity, however, did not improve. Eighteen months later
the left eye was similarly affected.
Neurological examination
Examination revealed fixed kyphosis of the upper and hyperlordosis
of the lower spine; the paravertebral muscles were stiff and hyper-
trophic. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk in the lower extremities.
The remainder of the neurological examination was normal.
Imaging
Cranial computerized tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imag-
ing (MRI) of the cranium and spine, and thoracic myelography were
all normal. X-rays of the spine showed signs of scoliosis and decal-
cification of the lumbar vertebrae.
The patient died in 1997, about 12 h after a spasm-induced fall
involving head trauma. Autopsy was not performed.

segments.text:
Results
Ophthalmological examination and follow-up
Upon admission in February 1996, visual acuity was 0.16
in the right eye and 0.6 in the left eye. Despite aggressive
immunosuppressive treatment with 1.v. steroids and meth-
otrexate, progression of visual loss in the left eye could
not be prevented. By May 1996 visual acuity of the left
eye had dropped to 0.3, and by August 1996 it was down
to 0.16. Visual acuity of both eyes then remained at 0.16.

Biomicroscopy and fluorescein angiography were nor-
mal on the initial evaluation and on follow-ups in May
and August 1996.
Static (Tiibingen Automatic Perimeter) and kinetic
(Goldmann) perimetry revealed a central scotoma of
about 10 deg in both eyes.
Colour discrimination, as examined by Ishihara’s col-
our plates, the Heidelberg anomaloscope and the Farns-
worth Panel D 15 test revealed a red-green deficit. Colour
discrimination was only moderately affected on the left
eye when the patient presented in February 1996 and pro-
gressively worsened.
ERG-recordings
The results of the ERG recordings are presented in
Figs. 14 and VEP recordings are summarized in Fig. 5.
Recordings of the right eye were abnormal at all times.
Recordings of the left eye showed gradual deterioration.
Abnormal electro-ocular responses were initially noted
on the pattern ERG (Fig. 1) and on photopic ERG
(Fig. 2), which revealed abnormal a- and b-waves in re-
sponse to photopic single red flash. Scotopic responses
(Fig. 3) became pathologic only later on. Increasingly ab-
normal flicker responses (Fig. 4) and the progressive im-
pairment of the photopic responses (Fig. 2) reflect the
progressive deterioration.
VEP recordings
On the first examination in October 1994, stimulation of
the left eye evoked a normal cortical potential, whereas
an attenuated VEP with normal latency was evoked from
the right. Repeated investigations revealed a mild but pro-
gressive slowing of the right eye VEP. VEPs for the left
eye remained normal until March 1996, when they first
desynchronised with a W shape. By the patient’s last visit
in August 1997, VEPs were about equally delayed and at-
tenuated on both sides. The progressive deterioration of
visual function is shown in Fig. 5.
Laboratory investigations
Standard serological studies, glucose tolerance tests and
repeat spinal taps yielded normal results except for one
oligoclonal band in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) on the
second tap in 1996. Norepinephrine, epinephrine and do-
pamine levels in the plasma and the CSF were within nor-
mal ranges. High levels of autoantibodies to both iso-
forms of GAD were present in patient’s serum
(167 432 U anti-GAD65 and 792 U anti-GAD67, RIA)
and to GAD65 in the CSF (2495 U, RIA).
Assessment of antiretinal antibodies
Indirect immunofluorescence revealed strong reactivity of
the macaque retinal inner plexiform layer and weaker
